clue.text: Pretentious woman with plenty of brass?

definitions.note: read literally: a lady with lots of money

blocks.note: first meaning: a snooty woman who gives herself airs
second meaning, read literally: a lady rich in money, since in northern English slang muck and brass both mean cash

explanation.surface: A snobbish woman who is also rather brazen and cheeky.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying 'where there's muck there's brass' links dirt and money; read the name literally and she is a lady loaded with muck, that is, brass.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is a British colloquial term for a woman who gives herself airs and behaves as though she were grand.

clue.text: The same lousy characters surrounding this symbol of Nazi retribution

indicators.note: surrounding says one set of letters goes around another, holding it inside

blocks.note: lice are the creatures that make one lousy
id. is short for idem, Latin for the same

explanation.surface: A grim note that the same verminous people encircled this emblem of Nazi vengeance.
explanation.walkthrough: LI(ID)CE: LIDICE was the Czech village razed in 1942 in reprisal for the assassination of Heydrich.
explanation.definitionFit: The village was destroyed and its men shot as a reprisal, so it stands as an emblem of Nazi revenge.

clue.text: Might cavil as devoted disputant

indicators.note: might hints at what the following letters could become if rearranged, a possible form rather than the given one

blocks.note: fourteen letters taken as written to be shuffled

explanation.surface: A keen arguer might quibble devotedly.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface describes the answer too: such a person quibbles devotedly for argument's sake.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who takes the opposing side purely to test an argument is a professional contrarian, a person who disputes.

clue.text: Othello left flat out in this part of the distillery

indicators.note: out suggests something disordered or put out of place, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: Othello is Shakespeare's Moor of Venice
L is the usual abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's tragic hero lies flat out drunk in a corner of the whisky distillery.
explanation.walkthrough: M(ALTFL)OOR: the jumbled letters of left-abbreviation plus flat sit inside the Moor.
explanation.definitionFit: Barley is spread to germinate on this floor when making malt for whisky, so it is one area of a distillery.

clue.text: About to consume alco-pop, saw a wasteful way out of Rome

indicators.note: to pop is to burst, so the word before it is broken up and its letters scattered
consuming means swallowing something whole, so one piece takes another inside it

blocks.note: ca. is short for circa, Latin for about
taken as written, to be jumbled
a saw is an old saying, a maxim
taken as written

explanation.surface: A warning that a drinker downing alcopops ends up with an inelegant exit from Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: C(LOAC)A + MAXIM + A. The answer is the great sewer of ancient Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: The Great Drain carried the city's waste into the Tiber, literally a channel by which refuse left Rome.

clue.text: Play opens here, with a battle

blocks.note: first meaning, read cryptically: a play begins at Act I
second meaning: fighting, combat

explanation.surface: A drama that begins with a fight scene.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as ACT I ON: the first act is on, which is where any play opens.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers who see combat are said to see this, the military word for fighting in battle.

clue.text: Influence cast after May 31

definitions.note: a noun: the garment one casts off

blocks.note: first meaning: power or weight, especially political
second meaning: an old word for a piece of clothing, from the proverb about not shedding it until May is out

explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'Ne'er cast a clout till May be out' warns not to shed warm clothes too early; a clout is an old word for a garment.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with power or sway is said to carry weight, and the same word is slang for pull or leverage.

clue.text: Glider could freeze fish

blocks.note: to ice is to freeze or chill
the skate is a flat fish like a ray

explanation.surface: A gliding creature might be frozen like a fish on a slab.
explanation.definitionFit: The bladed boot slides smoothly across a rink, so it is something that glides along.

clue.text: Piggy-wig controlled with this shilling's worth?

definitions.text: Piggy-wig controlled with this shilling's worth?

blocks.note: surface reading: a device for leading a pig about the farm
setter's reading: in Lear's The Owl and the Pussy-cat, the Piggy-wig sells the ring at the end of his snout for one shilling

explanation.surface: A pig being led around by a cheap little fitting.
explanation.walkthrough: Lear's poem has a Piggy-wig 'with a ring at the end of his nose', which he sells for one shilling so the owl and cat can marry; a shilling was an old British coin.
explanation.definitionFit: Farmers fit a metal hoop through a bull's or pig's snout so the animal can be led and controlled.

clue.text: Rocker's rival dwelt around here: what wickedness!

indicators.note: turning around means facing the other way, so the words are read from back to front

blocks.note: in 1960s Britain, mods and rockers were rival youth gangs
to dwell is to live

explanation.surface: The rocker's enemy once lived nearby, and what a wicked place it was.
explanation.walkthrough: Mods (scooters, sharp suits) and rockers (motorbikes, leather) fought on British beaches in the 1960s.
explanation.definitionFit: The realm or condition of devils is the state of evil itself, hence wickedness.

clue.text: Eager as the North Wind

blocks.note: an eager, more often spelt eagre, is a tidal wave surging up a river, a bore
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone as keen as a gust from the north.
explanation.walkthrough: Eager looks like keen, but it is a variant spelling of eagre, the tidal surge on rivers such as the Trent.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the god who personifies the cold wind from the north bears this name.

clue.text: The art of the Enigma Variations?

definitions.text: The art of the Enigma Variations?

blocks.clueFragment: The art of the Enigma Variations?
blocks.note: surface reading: the musical craft of Elgar's orchestral work
setter's reading: the German Enigma machine, whose many settings produced endless variations of secret code

explanation.surface: A question about the musical skill behind Elgar's famous orchestral piece.
explanation.walkthrough: The Enigma was the German wartime cipher machine broken at Bletchley Park.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing and breaking secret codes is the discipline studied by cipher experts, an art or science of hidden messages.

clue.text: He solved Turandot's riddle with some musical affectation

indicators.note: some means only part of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: An opera hero cracked the princess's puzzle with a touch of musical flourish.
explanation.definitionFit: In Puccini's opera the unknown prince answers the princess's three riddles and so wins her hand.

clue.text: Pinter's tender scene shot again in the car

indicators.note: in says one piece is placed inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
a scene filmed a second time is a retake

explanation.surface: A film director reshoots an affectionate Pinter scene in a car.
explanation.walkthrough: CA(RETAKE)R: the answer is Harold Pinter's play, and also a person who tends a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A tender is someone who looks after something, as a janitor does a building, and the word is also the title of a Pinter play.

clue.text: "The Lettuce-Wiper, Oil-Changer and Ant-Destroyer" - that's some magazine!

indicators.note: a changer alters the order of what comes before it, here the word oil
a destroyer wrecks the word before it, breaking it into a new order

blocks.note: cos is a variety of lettuce
a mop is used for wiping
oil, jumbled
ant, jumbled

explanation.surface: A mock title of three odd household devices, offered as the name of a strange periodical.
explanation.definitionFit: The title is a famous glossy women's monthly, so it is an example of a magazine.

clue.text: Sweetener might lose value

indicators.note: might hints at what the following words could turn into, a possible rearrangement

blocks.note: taken as written, to be shuffled

explanation.surface: A warning that a sugar substitute could become worth less.
explanation.definitionFit: It is another name for fructose, the fruit sugar, which is used to sweeten foods.

clue.text: Boss taking a lead from Bill Sykes?

definitions.text: taking a lead from Bill Sykes?
definitions.note: a description of the dog, not a synonym

blocks.note: first meaning: the raised centre of a shield or target

blocks.clueFragment: taking a lead from Bill Sykes?
blocks.note: second meaning: Sikes's dog in Dickens's Oliver Twist, walked on a lead by its master

explanation.walkthrough: Boss looks like a manager, but here it is the knob at the centre of a shield. Bill Sikes is the brutal villain of Oliver Twist.
explanation.definitionFit: A boss is a central stud or knob, and the middle of a dartboard or target has the same name; the dog in Dickens also bears it.

clue.text: See 2
King sat reluctantly nude at first: so what's wrong with the photograph?

indicators.note: doing something reluctantly means going about it awkwardly, so the next word comes out jumbled
at first places the following piece at the front of the chain

blocks.note: nude, jumbled
Rex is Latin for king, as on old coins
a model who sat for a portrait posed

explanation.surface: A monarch reluctantly posed naked for a picture, and something has gone wrong with the print.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture given too little light comes out dark and murky, which is a common photographic fault.

clue.text: Waller's rising note: I'll hear it in the Hebrides

definitions.text: I'll hear it in the Hebrides

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading upward, from bottom to top

blocks.note: Fats Waller was the American jazz pianist
fa is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A jazz pianist's ascending note is something one will hear among Scottish islands.
explanation.walkthrough: The island is home to Fingal's Cave, whose sea sounds inspired Mendelssohn's Hebrides overture.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the small Inner Hebridean island of Fingal's Cave, where the echoing waves are famous to listen to.

clue.text: Lyrical, possibly Shakespearian (except Richard IV's missing)

indicators.note: IV is the Roman four, and missing says the fourth letter is dropped

blocks.note: bar means except, as in 'all bar one'
Dick is a pet form of Richard

explanation.surface: Musing on Shakespeare's history plays, noting that a Richard IV is absent from the canon.
explanation.walkthrough: There was never a King Richard IV; the Roman numeral instead tells you which letter to drop.
explanation.definitionFit: A bard is a poet, and Shakespeare is the Bard, so the adjective means poetic or song-like.

clue.text: Smart performer once could be male relation

indicators.note: could be suggests the following letters might form something else when rearranged

blocks.note: M is the standard abbreviation for male
taken as written

explanation.surface: A clever entertainer of old might turn out to be a male relative.
explanation.walkthrough: Smart is not clever here: Billy Smart's Circus was a famous British travelling circus.
explanation.definitionFit: A big-cat act was a staple of the old travelling circus, so such a trainer was a classic circus performer.

clue.text: Bird-man's tribute

blocks.note: the tit is a small songbird
a man is referred to as he

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher's offering of praise.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenth of produce paid to the church was a levy or payment, the old sense of tribute.

clue.text: Extremist usurping Lenin, Trotsky, Rasputin and their leaders

indicators.note: leaders are those at the front, so the opening letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: the opening letters of these five words

explanation.surface: A radical seizing power from famous Russian revolutionary figures.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is used as a noun for a hardliner who holds the most radical views in a party.

clue.text: René has lost the Benefits Agency: what's his game?

indicators.note: has lost says the named body is taken away from the philosopher's surname, leaving the rest

blocks.note: René Descartes, the French philosopher
the DSS, Department of Social Security, ran British state benefits

explanation.surface: A Frenchman cut off by the welfare office, and someone wonders what he is playing at.
explanation.walkthrough: René is not any Frenchman but Descartes; strike out D, S and S and what is left is the card game.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a nineteenth-century French card game for two players in which cards may be thrown out and replaced.

clue.text: Dined at the club? On the contrary, indulged!

indicators.note: on the contrary says the two pieces go the opposite way round from the order given

blocks.note: a spoon is an old lofted golf club
to dine is to be fed

explanation.surface: Someone asks if you ate at the club and is told no, you were pampered.
explanation.walkthrough: Club looks like a gentlemen's club but is a golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: A child given everything without effort is pampered, so the word means spoiled or indulged.

clue.text: Crippen's Ethel changed parts and turned side

indicators.note: changed parts says the two halves of the name swap places
turned means faced the other way, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: Ethel Le Neve was the mistress of the murderer Dr Crippen

explanation.surface: The murderer's lover swapped roles and turned against him.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap LE and NEVE to get NEVELE, then read it backwards. Crippen fled to Canada with her in 1910.
explanation.definitionFit: A football or cricket team has that many players, so the number is used as a noun for a team.

clue.text: Like Simon, the cross-bearer, a cynic about to convert

indicators.note: to convert is to change form, so the letters are reworked

blocks.note: taken as written
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A sceptic is on the point of conversion, like the man who carried Christ's cross.
explanation.walkthrough: Simon of Cyrene carried the cross for Jesus; the Cynics and Cyrenaics were also rival Greek schools.
explanation.definitionFit: Simon came from Cyrene in North Africa, so he was by origin a native of that city.
